summary: Describes the abstract service interface that applications see for dynamic multicast address allocation. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: It is the order form that programs fill in to ask for a group address.

questions: how do applications request multicast addresses
subtitle: How applications request, manage, and release multicast group addresses.

tldr.problem: Applications need a standard way to ask for multicast addresses for temporary group communication, but no abstract interface existed.
tldr.mechanism: Define an abstract service interface (not tied to any programming language) with operations to allocate addresses for a specified lifetime, extend or shorten that lifetime, deallocate, query available scopes, and check how scopes nest.
tldr.outcome: This abstract API guides concrete implementations in operating systems and multicast allocation servers, making application code portable across different systems.

facts.label: Lease property: lifetime
facts.value: Duration for which allocation is guaranteed

facts.label: Async notification
facts.value: Not required; apps check lifetime proactively

today: This abstract API is Informational status and remains the conceptual foundation for multicast address allocation in operating systems and protocols that implement this service.

sections.title: The Multicast Address Allocation Problem
sections.content:
Multicast is a way for one sender to reach many receivers using a single address (like a broadcast). Applications create temporary multicast groups and need to obtain a unique multicast address for that group. The challenge is defining a standard interface that applications can use, independent of the operating system or the underlying allocation server implementation.

This RFC is informational; it does not define a network protocol. Instead, it describes what services the allocation system must provide to applications, in abstract terms. Actual operating system APIs and network protocols (like MADCAP) are built on top of this abstract interface.
sections.eli5: Lots of things want to start a multicast group, and they need a system that hands out group addresses. This RFC describes what that system should be able to do from the application's point of view.

sections.title: Data Types and Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC defines abstract data types: an AddressFamily (IPv4 or IPv6), a MulticastAddress (the actual group address), an AddressFamily (IPv4 or IPv6), a Scope (an administrative region where multicast works, like 'organization-local' or 'global'), and a Lease (the result of an allocation, containing the addresses, family, lifetime, and start time).

A Time value specifies when an allocation begins and when it expires. Scopes can nest: traffic sent to an address in a small scope might be reachable by hosts in a larger scope. A NestingRelationship describes whether two scopes nest, overlap, or are completely separate.
sections.eli5: The system needs to know: what kind of addresses (IPv4 or IPv6), where they can be used (a scope), how long they last, and how different scopes relate to each other.

sections.title: Allocating and Managing Addresses
sections.content:
An application calls alloc_multicast_addr specifying the address family, the scope where the group will operate, and its desired range of addresses and lifetimes. The allocation system returns a lease with the allocated addresses and their guaranteed lifetime. During the lifetime, the system makes a best-effort guarantee not to allocate those addresses to others.

Once allocated, an application can call change_multicast_addr_lifetime to extend or shorten the lifetime (which may fail). It can call deallocate_multicast_addr to explicitly release addresses. When addresses expire (their lifetime is up), the application must be prepared to either stop using them or allocate new ones. The RFC stresses that applications cannot rely on asynchronous notification of expiration; they must check the lease's lifetime and plan accordingly.
sections.eli5: The application asks 'can I have a group address that lasts for 2 hours?' The system either gives it a lease or says no. Later, the app can ask to extend the time or give it back.

sections.title: Querying Scopes and Nesting
sections.content:
Applications can query get_multicast_addr_scopes to learn what scopes are available on the system (e.g., link-local, organization-local, global). They can call get_scope_name to get a human-readable name for a scope in their preferred language (using language tags from RFC 1766).

To understand scope topology, applications can call get_scope_nesting_state to learn how a set of scopes nest relative to each other, get_larger_scopes to find scopes that encompass a given scope, and get_smaller_scopes to find nested scopes. This helps applications understand which group addresses are reachable in which parts of the network.
sections.eli5: The application can ask 'what regions exist on my network?' and 'can people in Europe see the group in the Americas scope?'

sections.title: Advance Allocation and Future Start Times
sections.content:
An application can allocate addresses to begin at a future time. For example, a conference program that starts in two weeks can allocate addresses now but request they not become active until the conference starts. This avoids wasting address space by reserving addresses for a long period.

An allocation request specifies minDesiredStartTime and maxDesiredStartTime (a time range) and minDesiredLifetime and maxDesiredLifetime (a duration range). The allocation system returns the actual start time and lifetime it granted. If the request cannot be satisfied, it may return TRY_LATER with a suggested time to retry.
sections.eli5: You can book a group address months in advance, and it will not be available for anyone else until right before your event starts.
